topics: Members of a Family
A family has parents, grandparents, brothers and sisters and other elders; relatives who live away are family too — related ...
Animals in Our Family
Animals like Shiru the dog can be members of a family
Types of Families
A family can have a few or many members, so families can be big or small
Fun Together
Family members of all ages enjoy time together — they play games, sing songs, laugh and eat together
Helping Each Other
In a family everyone does some work: we share the day-to-day work of the home and give special care to those who need it — that ...

items: A family has parents, grandparents, brothers and sisters and other elders; relatives who live away are family too — related through our mother or father. Family members love and take care of each other.
Family members love us, care for us and support us.
A family can have parents, grandparents, brothers, sisters and other elders.
Relatives who live away are related through our mother or father.
Animals like Shiru the dog can be members of a family. Families love and care for animals, trees and plants — we share food with animals and never hurt or tease them.
Animals can be family members.
Share food with animals; never hurt or tease them.
Families also care for trees and plants.
A family can have a few or many members, so families can be big or small. Families are different, and every family is special.
A family can have a few or many members.
Big or small, every family is special.
Family members of all ages enjoy time together — they play games, sing songs, laugh and eat together.
Families play, sing, laugh and eat together.
Grandparents teach us their games and songs.
In a family everyone does some work: we share the day-to-day work of the home and give special care to those who need it — that is how family members show love.
Everyone in a family does some work.
We give special care to grandparents, small children and the sick.
Helping is a way of showing love and care.
Friends and neighbours also love us and support us: we play, celebrate and learn together, and we care for many people who are not in our family.
Friends and neighbours also love and support us.
We learn from each other.
We care for many others who are not in our family.
Wrong: Only the people who live in our house are our family. Right: Relatives who live away, related through our mother or father, are also our family
Wrong: Teasing an animal is just fun. Right: Teasing hurts and scares animals — they feel pain and fear just like us
Wrong: A big family is better than a small family. Right: Families are different and we love them all — every family is special
Wrong: Only children play games. Right: Dadaji plays with the children and Dadiji sings with them — elders join the fun too
Wrong: Housework is only mother's job. Right: Bela's parents share all the housework, and everyone in the family does some work
Wrong: Everyone we call Mausi is a relative. Right: Kusum Mausi is mother's close friend, like a sister — not a relative, yet close like family

sol_items: Who are the members in Bela family?: Father, mother, Dadiji, Dadaji, Banku Bhaiya and Bela herself.
Would you call Bela family big or small?: Big, because it has many members.
Why should we not hurt or tease animals?: Animals feel pain and fear just like us and they trust us.
How do family members show love and care for each : By helping each other, sharing work, looking after the sick and playing together.
We care for many others not in our family. Who are they...: Friends, neighbours, animals, plants and people who help us; we care by being kind, sharing and helping.
Find and circle five games words in the grid: Read the words from the letter grid in the book.
imp_items: Who are relatives?
Family members who may not live with us, related through our mother or father
Your mother sister lives in another city. Is she part of your family? Why?
Yes, she is a relative related to us through our mother
Name the members of Bela family.
Father, mother, Dadiji, Dadaji, Banku Bhaiya and Bela
Name two animals other than a dog that can be part of a family.
Cow and parrot
Why should we not hurt or tease animals?
They feel pain and fear like us
Is a big family better than a small family? Why?
No; families are different and every family is special

topics: Preparing for the Mela
Before a trip we plan who is coming and how each person will travel, pack what we need (water bottles, a bag) and get ready on ...

A sketch is a simple drawing of places and the roads joining them; by reading its labels and following the roads we can find ...

items: Before a trip we plan who is coming and how each person will travel, pack what we need (water bottles, a bag) and get ready on time.
A trip is going somewhere together; first we get ready.
Plan: who comes, how we go, what we carry, when we leave, where we meet.

notes.h: Travelling Safely by Bus and Other Transport
items: We travel by different kinds of transport — bus, train, autorickshaw and more — and stay safe by walking carefully on the road and following the rules inside the bus.
Transport: bus, train, autorickshaw, cycle, car … — each suits a different trip.
Road: walk carefully, look both ways. Bus: sit, stay still, hands and head inside.
A sketch is a simple drawing of places and the roads joining them; by reading its labels and following the roads we can find places, see which is closer and trace a route.
Find a place: read the labels.
Find the way: follow the roads and name the places you pass.
A mela is a big fair with stalls to shop at, rides, shows and food; we enjoy it with clean habits — wash hands before eating and put waste in the dustbin.
A mela has stalls, rides, shows and food.
Wash hands before eating; waste goes in the dustbin.

notes.h: Safety and Help at the Mela
items: A mela has a big crowd, so help is kept ready — a map, an ambulance, a police jeep, a fire engine and a Lost and Found booth with volunteers — and police officers with police dogs keep people safe.
Big crowds need help kept ready: ambulance, fire engine, police, Lost and Found.
Lost? Go to the Lost and Found booth or a police officer.
Elders like Dadiji can enjoy a trip too when we help them — invite them, hold their hand, help them climb in, give them a seat and bring a wheelchair.
Invite elders, walk at their speed, help them in, give them a seat, bring a wheelchair.
Children can care for elders too.
Wrong: Getting ready only means wearing nice clothes. Right: It also means planning who comes, how we go, what we carry and leaving on time
Wrong: It is fine to put a hand out of the bus window to feel the wind. Right: Vehicles pass very close — keep hands and head inside the window
Wrong: A sketch must look exactly like a photo. Right: A sketch shows only the important places and roads, drawn simply with labels
Wrong: A mela is only for buying things. Right: A mela also has rides, shows, food and time together with family and friends
Wrong: An ambulance or fire engine at the mela means something bad has already happened. Right: They are kept ready in case something happens in the big crowd
Wrong: Elders whose legs hurt should just stay at home. Right: With help — a hand, a seat, a wheelchair — they can enjoy the trip too

sol_items: How do you prepare yourself for a trip?: Plan where we are going, who is coming and how we will travel; pack water and a bag with what we need; be ready on time.
What is the purpose of the Lost and Found booth?: To help lost people, especially children, find their family and to keep lost things until the owner comes.
What is the role of the police dog?: It helps the police keep people safe; it is trained to search using its strong sense of smell.
Why are fire engines and ambulances present at a m: They are kept ready in case something happens in the big crowd.
Find and circle Rohit and Sneha house on the sketc: Find the label on the sketch and circle it.
Find and circle Nita and Radha house on the sketch: Find the label on the sketch and circle it.
imp_items: Name two things to carry on a trip.
Water bottle and a bag
How do you prepare yourself for a trip?
Plan where, who and how; pack water and a bag; check things and be ready on time
Name three kinds of transport.
Bus, train, autorickshaw
Why should we keep hands and head inside the bus window?
Other vehicles pass very close and can hurt us
Rohit father asks for five full and four half tickets. Why?
There are nine people; one ticket for each, half for children
What is a sketch?
A simple drawing of places and roads, with labels

topics: A Visit to Relatives in the Mountains
Rishi travels by bus from Jammu with his parents to a small village near the Himalayas to visit his Mama, Mami and cousins — ...
Travelling Safely
We travel by many modes of transport — bus, train, car, bicycle or on foot — and in each we follow simple safety rules so the ...
Road Signboards
Road signboards use a picture instead of many words to tell everyone on the road what to watch out for or what not to do
Spring: A Celebration of Nature
After the harsh winter comes spring: the sun shines brightly, flowers bloom, grass grows and trees get new leaves — so spring is ...
Spring Festivals of India
People in different parts of India welcome spring with flower festivals: the Kashmir tulip festival, placing buransh and mustard ...

We celebrate festivals in every season, each with its own special food and dresses — and every festival brings families, ...

notes.h: A Visit to Relatives in the Mountains
items: Rishi travels by bus from Jammu with his parents to a small village near the Himalayas to visit his Mama, Mami and cousins — relatives who live far away are still our family, and visiting them is a joy.
Mama = mother's brother; Mami = Mama's wife; their children are our cousins.
Hill roads have hairpin turns; near villages roads may be narrow mud roads.
Himalayas = 'home of snow'; Mount Everest (about 8,848 m) is in Nepal.
We travel by many modes of transport — bus, train, car, bicycle or on foot — and in each we follow simple safety rules so the journey stays happy.
We travel by many modes of transport.
In a bus: keep head, hands and arms inside.
On the road: footpath, zebra crossing, look both ways; on a bicycle: helmet and keep left.
Road signboards use a picture instead of many words to tell everyone on the road what to watch out for or what not to do.
Signboards give a message with a picture.
Some signs warn us to be careful; red circle-with-line signs say 'do not'.
After the harsh winter comes spring: the sun shines brightly, flowers bloom, grass grows and trees get new leaves — so spring is a celebration of nature.
Spring comes after winter.
Signs of spring: bright sun, blooming flowers, growing grass, new leaves.
Garden flowers Rishi knew: rose, marigold, hibiscus. Spring and festival flowers: tulip, buransh (red), mustard, amaltas (yellow).
People in different parts of India welcome spring with flower festivals: the Kashmir tulip festival, placing buransh and mustard flowers at doorsteps, Vishu in Kerala and Sarhul in Jharkhand.
Kashmir — tulip festival; Rishi's place — buransh and mustard at doorsteps; Kerala — Vishu; Jharkhand — Sarhul.
Spring festivals use flowers and thank nature.

notes.h: Festivals Through the Seasons: Food and Dresses
items: We celebrate festivals in every season, each with its own special food and dresses — and every festival brings families, relatives and neighbours together.
There are festivals in every season.
Each festival has special food and dresses.
Festivals bring families and neighbours together.
Wrong: Mama is mother's father. Right: Mama is mother's BROTHER; Mami is Mama's wife
Wrong: It is fine to put your hand out of the bus window to feel the wind. Right: Always keep your head, hands and arms inside — passing vehicles, poles and trees can hurt you
Wrong: A red line across a picture means 'do this'. Right: A red circle with a line across means DO NOT do it (no horn, no U-turn)
Wrong: Spring comes right after summer. Right: Spring comes after the harsh winter
Wrong: All of India celebrates spring with the same festival. Right: Each place has its own spring festival — tulip festival, Rishi's spring festival, Vishu, Sarhul
Wrong: A festival is not real without new clothes and many dishes. Right: Families celebrate in their own ways; being together is the heart of a festival

sol_items: What safety measures should you take while travell: Keep head, hands and arms inside the bus, sit properly, hold elders and small children, wear seat belts in a car.
Safety while riding a bicycle and walking on the r: On a bicycle wear a helmet and keep left. When walking use the footpath and zebra crossing and look both ways.
Match the road signboards with their meanings: Match each sign with its message, for example a red circle with a line across a horn means no horn.
Match the festival foods with the festivals: For example Sadya - Onam.
Does everyone celebrate festivals with special food and...: Not everyone; families celebrate in their own ways and being together matters most.
Different modes of transport used during travel: Bus, train, car, bicycle, and walking.
imp_items: Who is Mama?
Mother brother
Who are Chiya and Nonikaa to Rishi?
His cousins
What does the word Himalayas mean?
Home of snow
Why should we keep our hands inside the bus?
Vehicles, poles or trees passing close by can hurt an arm outside
Why do signboards use pictures?
Everyone understands a picture quickly, even from far away
What does a red circle with a line across a picture mean?
It means do not do it

topics: Parts of a Plant
Every plant has parts — roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds — and each part has its own job
Trees
Trees are big plants with a big trunk of wood, many branches with leaves, and roots that go deep into the soil
Shrubs
Shrubs are medium-sized, bushy plants with several woody stems and branches growing close to the ground
Herbs and Grasses
Herbs are smaller plants with soft stems that never become woody; grasses are a kind of herb with thin flat leaves and hollow ...
Climbers and Creepers
Climbers and creepers have thin, flexible stems that cannot stand up; climbers grow up on a support, creepers spread along the ...
Make Friends with a Plant
We get to know a plant by caring for it every day and observing how its leaves, flowers and fruits change over time
Exploring Plants with Our Senses
Leaves of different plants have different colours, shapes, sizes, textures and smells; fruits have smells too — we can tell ...

items: Every plant has parts — roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds — and each part has its own job.
Six parts: root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed
Roots are under the soil; the other parts are above it
The flower comes first, then the fruit; the seeds are inside the fruit
Bark is the hard covering of a tree trunk
Trees are big plants with a big trunk of wood, many branches with leaves, and roots that go deep into the soil.
Tree = big woody trunk + many branches with leaves + deep roots
Mango, banyan, peepal, jamun are trees
Shrubs are medium-sized, bushy plants with several woody stems and branches growing close to the ground.
Shrub = medium size + several woody stems close to the ground
Dal comes from seeds of shrubs
Herbs are smaller plants with soft stems that never become woody; grasses are a kind of herb with thin flat leaves and hollow stems.
Herb = small + soft stem that never becomes woody
Grass = a herb with thin flat leaves and hollow stems
Grains are seeds of grasses; sugarcane and bamboo are tall grasses
Climbers and creepers have thin, flexible stems that cannot stand up; climbers grow up on a support, creepers spread along the ground.
Climbers and creepers: thin, flexible stems
Climber grows UP on a support; creeper grows ALONG the ground
We get to know a plant by caring for it every day and observing how its leaves, flowers and fruits change over time.
Choose, name, water and protect your plant friend
Observe leaves, flowers and fruits and record with date, month and weather
Plants change over time
Leaves of different plants have different colours, shapes, sizes, textures and smells; fruits have smells too — we can tell plants apart by looking, touching and smelling.
Look: colour, shape, size
Touch: texture (rough or smooth)
Smell: leaves and fruits have their own smells
Wrong: A tree trunk is not a stem — only small plants have stems. Right: The trunk IS the tree's stem — big, thick and woody, covered by bark
Wrong: Every tall plant is a tree. Right: Bamboo and sugarcane are tall but they are grasses; a tree has a big trunk of wood
Wrong: A shrub is just a baby tree. Right: A shrub stays medium-sized and has several woody stems, not one big trunk
Wrong: Grass is not a herb — it is something different. Right: Grasses are kinds of herbs
Wrong: Climbers and creepers have strong stems. Right: Their stems are thin and flexible — they cannot stand up by themselves
Wrong: A plant looks the same every day — it does not change. Right: New leaves grow and change colour, old leaves turn brown and fall, and flowers turn into fruits

sol_items: What are these shrubs called in your mother tongue: Write the names in your own language.
Snake gourd: A climber, because it climbs on a support.
What do you call snake gourd in your language?: Write the name in your language.
Name marigold, neem and ber in your language; say tree,...: Marigold is a herb, neem is a tree, ber is a small tree or shrub.
Observe your plant friend leaves, flowers and fruits an...: Record many, a few or none, colour and shape, with the date, month and weather.
New leaves? Do colours change? Do old brown leaves fall...: New leaves grow and change colour, old brown leaves fall, flowers turn into fruits.
imp_items: Which part of a plant is under the soil?
The roots
Name the six parts of a plant.
Root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit and seed
How does the root help a plant?
It holds the plant in the soil and takes in water
What is the trunk of a tree?
Its stem, big and woody, covered by bark
Is tulsi a tree or a shrub? Why?
A shrub, with several woody stems close to the ground
Why is mint called a herb?
Its stem is soft and green and never becomes woody

subject: EVS
title: Plants and Animals Live Together
intro: In Class 3 EVS Chapter 5, Plants and Animals Live Together, the topics are: Animals Live On, Around and Under Plants, what is soil made of?, creatures living in the soil, plants give food to animals, plants give shelter and a place to rest, sounds of birds. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Animals Live On, Around and Under Plants
Wherever there are plants, there are animals too — living on the plant, around it, and even under it in the soil
What Is Soil Made Of?
Soil is the topmost layer of the Earth's surface
Creatures Living in the Soil
Soil is a home
Plants Give Food to Animals
Many animals, birds and insects eat different parts of plants — leaves, grass, fruits and the nectar of flowers
Plants Give Shelter and a Place to Rest
Plants are homes too
Sounds of Birds
Many birds that live in trees can be known by their sounds

notes.h: Animals Live On, Around and Under Plants
items: Wherever there are plants, there are animals too — living on the plant, around it, and even under it in the soil.
ON the plant — leaves, flowers, branches, trunk, hollows, grass (grass is a plant too)
AROUND the plant — near it but not on it: bare ground, a rock, or the air close by
UNDER the plant — in the soil around its roots

Soil is the topmost layer of the Earth's surface. It is made of rocks broken into tiny pieces, old leaves, roots and stems, and living and dead animals — so soil can look, feel and smell different from place to place.
Soil = topmost layer of the Earth's surface
Rock pieces + old plant parts + animals = soil
Check soil by looking, touching and smelling

Soil is a home. Ants, termites, small beetles and grasshoppers move on its top layer; earthworms and millipedes come up when the soil is wet after rain; and seeds waiting in the soil sprout when it rains.
Some insects wait in the soil for the rains and then come out
Seeds can stay in the soil for a long time and sprout when it rains or they are watered
Plants often grow fresh new leaves after the rains (added) — note the month YOUR plant friend got new leaves
Many animals, birds and insects eat different parts of plants — leaves, grass, fruits and the nectar of flowers.
Leaves — camel, caterpillar
Grass — elephant
Fruits — monkey
Nectar — sunbird, butterfly

notes.h: Plants Give Shelter and a Place to Rest
items: Plants are homes too. Birds and animals use tree hollows, twigs and leaves to make nests and bring up their young ones, and use branches and leaves to hide, rest and shelter.
Animals use plants for FOOD, SHELTER and RESTING
Shelter = a home or nest, often to bring up young ones
Rest = a safe place to sit or sleep

Many birds that live in trees can be known by their sounds. Different birds make different sounds; cupping our ears and facing the sound helps us hear better; and we hear more bird sounds at some times of the day.
Cupped hands catch more sound and send it into the ear, so the sound is clearer (added)
Many birds call the most in the early morning, and again in the evening (added — check for yourself)
No bird sounds? Maybe too much noise, no trees nearby, or the hot middle of the day (added — find your own reason)
Wrong: Animals live only in forests and zoos. Right: Animals live near every plant — even a small plant in the school garden has ants, insects and birds
Wrong: Soil is just dust — nothing is in it. Right: Soil has rock pieces, old leaves, roots, stems and living and dead animals
Wrong: Earthworms and new plants come down from the sky with the rain. Right: They were already in the soil — the rain makes the soil wet, so worms come up and seeds sprout
Wrong: Butterflies eat leaves. Right: Caterpillars eat leaves; butterflies drink nectar from flowers
Wrong: Every bird's nest is made of twigs. Right: Owls and barbets use tree hollows; tailorbirds stitch leaves together
Wrong: All birds make the same sound. Right: Different birds make different sounds — a pigeon's 'gutru gu' is not a crow's 'caw'

sol_items: Why do these animals choose to live near plants?: Plants give them food, shelter and a place to rest.
A day after rain, is the soil different?: Yes, it is darker, damp and softer, with a stronger smell.
Is soil far from plants different from soil near your p...: Soil near plants has more leaves, roots and insects.
What small things do you notice in the soil?: Rock pieces, bits of leaves, roots and small insects.
In the monsoons, where do new plants and animals c: They were already in the soil as seeds, eggs and sleeping insects. They come out after the rain.
Cup your ears and face the bird sound: Yes, the sound becomes clearer.
imp_items: Which animal lives under the ground?
The earthworm
Why do animals choose to live near plants?
Plants give them food, shelter and a place to rest
What is soil?
The topmost layer of the Earth surface
What is soil made of?
Tiny rock pieces, old leaves, roots and stems, and living and dead animals
Where do the new plants and animals come from in the monsoons?
They were already in the soil as seeds and sleeping insects; rain wakes them
Which animals eat leaves, grass and fruits? One each.
Camel - leaves; elephant - grass; monkey - fruits

topics: Animals and Plants That Share Our Home
Some animals and plants live in our homes because we brought them; others came on their own
How Plants Help Us and Animals
Plants give animals and people food, shade, shelter, wood, fibre, medicine and fresh air — the mango tree is a home and a food ...
How Animals Help Plants and Us
Animals help plants by spreading their seeds and making the soil fertile with their waste; animals like cows, buffaloes and goats ...

Just as we get so much from plants and animals, we give them care, protection, water, food and shelter — with kindness, never ...

We become friends with animals and plants by watching them closely, talking to a plant friend and welcoming visiting birds, as ...

notes.h: Animals and Plants That Share Our Home
items: Some animals and plants live in our homes because we brought them; others came on their own. We may like some and not others, but we never hurt them.
We bring some animals and plants home.
Some come and live with us on their own.
We like some and not others — but we never hurt them.

notes.h: How Plants Help Us and Animals
items: Plants give animals and people food, shade, shelter, wood, fibre, medicine and fresh air — the mango tree is a home and a food store.
Plants give: fruit, vegetables, shade, shelter, wood, fibre, medicine, fresh air.
A tree can be a home for many animals.

notes.h: How Animals Help Plants and Us
items: Animals help plants by spreading their seeds and making the soil fertile with their waste; animals like cows, buffaloes and goats give us milk and loving company.
Animals help plants: spread seeds + make soil fertile.
Animals help us: milk + loving company.
So we respect animals and treat them with kindness, care and compassion.

notes.h: How We Care for Plants and Animals
items: Just as we get so much from plants and animals, we give them care, protection, water, food and shelter — with kindness, never hurting them.
We give: water, food, shelter, protection and care.
We treat animals with kindness, care and compassion.
Never hurt an animal, even if we are scared of it.

notes.h: Making Friends with Animals and Plants
items: We become friends with animals and plants by watching them closely, talking to a plant friend and welcoming visiting birds, as the children of Valparai do.
Watch an animal closely to know it.
Guess first, then watch.
Talk to a plant friend.
Welcome birds, like Valparai.
Wrong: Only pets live in our home. Right: Uninvited guests like ants, lizards and sparrows also share our home
Wrong: Plants only give us food. Right: Plants also give shade, shelter, wood, fibre, medicine and fresh air
Wrong: Animals only take from plants by eating them. Right: Animals also help plants — they spread seeds and make the soil fertile with their waste
Wrong: Plants and animals can look after themselves; they do not need us. Right: Animals and plants depend on us too — for water, food, shelter and protection
Wrong: Plants cannot be our friends because they cannot talk. Right: We can still talk to a plant friend, share our feelings and care for it

sol_items: Do you and your family take care of them?: Yes, we give them water and food.
Why do they come to your home?: For food, water and shelter.
What do you do when you do not like them?: I do not hurt them; I gently send them out or keep food covered.
How are we dependent on plants and animals?: Plants give us food, wood, fibre and fresh air; animals give us milk and company.
How do plants help animals?: They give food, shelter and shade.
How do animals help plants?: They spread seeds and make the soil fertile with their waste.
imp_items: Is a lizard on your wall brought in by you? Why?
No, it came on its own
Why do ants come to the kitchen?
To find food such as sugar and crumbs
Give two examples each of things we bring home and things that come on their own.
Brought: dog, potted plant. Uninvited: ants, lizards
Name two things we get from plants.
Fruits and wood
Write three ways in which plants help us and animals.
Food, shade and shelter
How does a monkey help a mango tree?
It eats the mango and drops the seed elsewhere so a new plant can grow

subject: EVS
title: Water — A Precious Gift
intro: In Class 3 EVS Chapter 7, Water — A Precious Gift, the topics are: Rain — Guessing and Observing It, where rainwater goes, how water reaches our homes, storing water, uses of water in daily life, saving water — reduce, reuse, keep it clean, every drop counts — sharing water. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Rain — Guessing and Observing It
Water comes down to Earth as rain
Where Rainwater Goes
Rainwater soaks into the soil, flows away into streams and rivers, collects in puddles, ponds, lakes, seas and oceans, or dries ...
How Water Reaches Our Homes
Water reaches our homes in many ways: through taps and pipes from a tank, from wells and borewells drawn up by a pulley or pump, ...
Storing Water
We store water because we do not get it all the time
Uses of Water in Daily Life
We need water for almost everything we do every day — drinking, cooking, bathing, brushing, washing and cleaning
Saving Water — Reduce, Reuse, Keep It Clean
After we use water it becomes dirty and cannot be used for drinking or cooking, but it can be reused for watering plants or ...
Every Drop Counts — Sharing Water
Water is considered sacred because we cannot survive without it

items: Water comes down to Earth as rain. We can guess when rain will come from clues in the sky and the air, and we can observe rain closely — how heavy, how big the drops, how fast, which direction, and whether its water is clean.
Water comes down to Earth as rain.
Clues in the sky help us guess rain, but a guess can be wrong.
We can observe rain: heavy/light, drop size, fast/slow, direction, clean/dirty.

Rainwater soaks into the soil, flows away into streams and rivers, collects in puddles, ponds, lakes, seas and oceans, or dries up in the sun. Water that soaks in is stored underground — the water in our wells comes from it.
Rainwater soaks in, flows away, collects, or dries up.
Water that soaks in fills underground water — our wells get water from it.
Streams join rivers; some water gathers in seas and oceans.
Water reaches our homes in many ways: through taps and pipes from a tank, from wells and borewells drawn up by a pulley or pump, carried by people from a river, lake or well, or brought by tankers.
Tap ← pipe ← tank ← bigger pipes ← source.
Wells and borewells: pulley, hand pump or electric pump.
Some people carry water from far away; tankers deliver it too.
We store water because we do not get it all the time. Long ago there were no pipes or taps, so people learned to make vessels; today we store water in vessels of clay, metal, glass and plastic.
We store water because we do not get it all the time.
Vessels are made of clay, metal, glass or plastic.
Long ago people made vessels because there were no taps.

notes.h: Uses of Water in Daily Life
items: We need water for almost everything we do every day — drinking, cooking, bathing, brushing, washing and cleaning. Water keeps things clean, which is very important for our health.
We use water for drinking, cooking, bathing, brushing, washing and cleaning.
Water keeps things clean — important for health.
Counting mugs shows how much water we use.

notes.h: Saving Water — Reduce, Reuse, Keep It Clean
items: After we use water it becomes dirty and cannot be used for drinking or cooking, but it can be reused for watering plants or flushing toilets. We should reduce our use of water, reuse it when possible, and not add too much soap or chemicals to it.
After use, water becomes dirty — not for drinking or cooking.
Reuse: plants, flushing toilets.
Reduce our use; do not add too much soap or chemicals.

Water is considered sacred because we cannot survive without it. In some dry places people walk long distances for it, so everyone should get clean drinking water anytime. We can share water with people, animals and birds — for example by making a birdbath.
Water is considered sacred — absolutely essential for our survival.
Share drinking water with people, animals and birds.
Birdbath: shallow, stones, fresh water, cleaned twice a week.
Wrong: Rainwater is always clean, so we can drink it straight away. Right: Collect it and look — rainwater can carry dust and dirt from the air and the roof
Wrong: Rainwater just disappears after the rain stops. Right: It goes somewhere: into the soil, into streams and rivers, into puddles, ponds and lakes, or into the air when it dries
Wrong: Water is made inside the tap. Right: The tap only lets water out; it comes through pipes from a tank
Wrong: Water comes all the time, so we never need to store it. Right: Pipelines can burst and supply can stop; stored water helps then
Wrong: We use water only for drinking. Right: We also use it for cooking, bathing, brushing, washing and cleaning
Wrong: Used water is useless — pour it all down the drain. Right: Reuse it for watering plants or flushing toilets

sol_items: Are there clues that help you guess if it will rain? As...: Yes: dark clouds, cool wind, and the smell of wet soil.
Write 2 clues it will rain and 2 clues it will not: Rain: dark clouds, cool wind. No rain: clear blue sky, bright sun.
Collect rainwater: It may look a little dirty because it carries dust from the air and roofs.
Find or make up songs about rain and sing them: Sing a rain song with friends.
Did the rain make you happy? Everyone?: It makes many happy, but it can trouble people with leaking roofs or floods.
Where did the rainwater go?: Into the soil, puddles, and flowing away to streams and rivers.
imp_items: What comes down but never goes up?
Rain
Name two clues that it may rain soon.
Dark clouds and a cool wind
Why might rain fall slanting?
The wind pushes the drops sideways
Where does a well get its water from?
From underground water, rain that soaked into the soil
Write three places rainwater goes.
Into the soil, into streams and rivers, and into puddles and ponds
Name three ways water is drawn from a well.
Pulley, hand pump, electric pump

subject: EVS
title: Food We Eat
intro: In Class 3 EVS Chapter 8, Food We Eat, the topics are: Tastes of Food, food in different seasons and places, why we need healthy food, why our body needs water, food from plants, food from animals, good food habits. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Tastes of Food
We all like different foods
Food in Different Seasons and Places
We eat different foods in different seasons — cool food and drinks in summer, warm food in winter, and the fruits of each season ...
Why We Need Healthy Food
We eat to have a strong and healthy body with energy
Why Our Body Needs Water
Our body needs a lot of water; we cannot live without it
Food from Plants
Much of our food comes from plants grown in fields
Food from Animals
Some foods are taken from animals — milk, curd, ghee, cheese, paneer, honey, eggs, meat
Good Food Habits
Good food habits care for others and for food: share food with a friend who has none, eat and share together, serve guests with ...

items: We all like different foods. Foods have different tastes — sweet, sour, salty, spicy, bitter and astringent — and a good meal can have many tastes together, like chhappan bhog.
Six tastes: sweet, sour, salty, spicy, bitter, astringent
Chhappan bhog = 56 items with all six tastes
We all have favourite foods — and our reasons are often the taste

notes.h: Food in Different Seasons and Places
items: We eat different foods in different seasons — cool food and drinks in summer, warm food in winter, and the fruits of each season — and people in different parts of India eat different dishes.
Hot summer → cool foods and drinks; cold winter → warm foods
Each season brings its own fruits and vegetables
Different places, different dishes
We eat to have a strong and healthy body with energy. Eating many kinds of food, cooked at home, gives a balanced diet — eating only one or two favourite foods is not enough.
We eat for energy, strength and health
Eat a variety: vegetables, fruits, grains, pulses, nuts
Home-cooked food is best
Many kinds of food in the right amounts = balanced diet
Our body needs a lot of water; we cannot live without it. When we sweat — in hot weather or while playing — we lose water, so we must drink water often.
We sweat in summer and when we play
Sweat = water leaving the body
Drink water frequently
'Water is life' — we cannot live without water
Much of our food comes from plants grown in fields. We eat different parts of plants — leaves, fruits, roots, stems and seeds.
Five plant parts we eat: leaves, fruits, roots, stems, seeds
Grains, pulses and nuts like almond and cashew are seeds
Crops are grown in fields

Some foods are taken from animals — milk, curd, ghee, cheese, paneer, honey, eggs, meat. Some dishes mix plant and animal ingredients (lassi), and a few ingredients — salt and water — come from neither.
Milk and things made from milk come from animals
Honey is made by bees
Salt and water: neither plant nor animal
Some dishes mix plant and animal ingredients

Good food habits care for others and for food: share food with a friend who has none, eat and share together, serve guests with care, do not waste food, and eat proper meals in the morning, afternoon and night.
Share food
Do not waste food
Eat together
Eat proper meals morning, afternoon, night
Wrong: Only sweet food is tasty food. Right: Sour, salty, spicy, bitter and astringent foods are tasty too — chhappan bhog mixes all six
Wrong: We get all fruits in every season. Right: Each fruit comes in its own season — mangoes and melons in summer, plenty of apples in winter
Wrong: If I eat my favourite food (only rice and potatoes) every day, I will be strong. Right: Rice and potatoes are good, but we must eat many other kinds of food too
Wrong: We need water only in summer. Right: Our body needs a lot of water every day; we drink more in summer because we sweat more
Wrong: Potato grows under the soil, so it is a root. Right: The book puts potato with stems — it grows underground but it is a stem; carrot, radish and beetroot are roots
Wrong: Honey comes from flowers, so it is plant food. Right: Bees make honey; the book lists honey among foods from animals

sol_items: Ask elders: To get energy, grow, stay strong and healthy.
Why do we need to eat healthy food?: It gives a strong, healthy body with energy.
Which of these foods should be part of a balanced : A variety: vegetables, fruits, grains, dal, milk and nuts.
List fruits, vegetables and special foods of summer and...: Summer: mango, melon, lassi. Winter: oranges, carrots, gajar halwa.
Which foods are grown in the fields? Write names o: Wheat, rice, maize, pulses and vegetables.
In what form are some of these foods cooked?: Wheat as roti, rice as cooked rice, pulses as dal.
imp_items: Which taste is karela?
Bitter (karva)
Name the six tastes of food.
Sweet, sour, salty, spicy, bitter and astringent
How many tastes are in chhappan bhog?
Six
Why do we eat seasonal foods?
They grow in that season and suit its weather
Why did Shirin fall sick often?
She ate only rice and potatoes, not a variety of food
Why do we drink more water in summer?
It is hot, we sweat and lose water

title: Staying Healthy and Happy
intro: In Class 3 EVS Chapter 9, Staying Healthy and Happy, the topics are: Keeping Our Body Clean, how we clean our teeth — datun and toothbrush, making a home-cleaner from orange and lemon peels, exercise and play — outdoors and indoors, playing safely, my daily routine, tracking my habits — health table and 24-hour circle. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Keeping Our Body Clean
Simple cleanliness habits — brushing teeth, taking a shower, combing hair, washing hands with soap and keeping nails trimmed and ...
How We Clean Our Teeth — Datun and Toothbrush
Long before toothbrushes, people in India cleaned their teeth with datun — fresh twigs of neem, babool or karanj chewed into a ...
Making a Home-Cleaner from Orange and Lemon Peels
Cleaning agents remove dirt and germs from kitchen slabs, furniture and bathrooms
Exercise and Play — Outdoors and Indoors
When we run and play we breathe faster and deeper, feel warm and sweat because exercise makes the heart work harder and better
Playing Safely
Fun must be safe: play in safe places like a park or schoolground, not on a busy road, a roof without railings or a construction ...
My Daily Routine
A daily routine is the list of things we do every day from waking up till going to sleep
Tracking My Habits — Health Table and 24-Hour Circle
Feelings like sleepy, hungry or tired are the body's way of telling us something is amiss

items: Simple cleanliness habits — brushing teeth, taking a shower, combing hair, washing hands with soap and keeping nails trimmed and clean — keep our body clean and free from diseases. Animals keep themselves clean too.
Clean body = fewer diseases
Five checks: teeth, shower, hair, hands with soap, nails
Animals keep clean in their own ways

notes.h: How We Clean Our Teeth — Datun and Toothbrush
items: Long before toothbrushes, people in India cleaned their teeth with datun — fresh twigs of neem, babool or karanj chewed into a brush. The modern idea of brushing came from this tradition.
Datun = twig of neem / babool / karanj
Chew → brush → clean teeth and massage gums
Modern brushing came from datun

notes.h: Making a Home-Cleaner from Orange and Lemon Peels
items: Cleaning agents remove dirt and germs from kitchen slabs, furniture and bathrooms. We can make our own eco-friendly all-purpose cleaner from orange or lemon peels and vinegar, just as people once used natural things like reetha and shikakai.
Peels + vinegar → sun 2 weeks → strain → 1 cup per bucket
Eco-friendly = made from natural things

notes.h: Exercise and Play — Outdoors and Indoors
items: When we run and play we breathe faster and deeper, feel warm and sweat because exercise makes the heart work harder and better. Outdoor games keep the body fit; indoor games like chess keep the mind active — both mind and body should be active.
Exercise → heart works harder and better
Outdoor games: body; indoor games: mind
Do a stamina activity at least twice a week
Fun must be safe: play in safe places like a park or schoolground, not on a busy road, a roof without railings or a construction site, and never go with or take things from strangers.
Safe: park, schoolground
Unsafe: busy road, roof without railings, construction site
Strangers: say NO and stay with a trusted adult

A daily routine is the list of things we do every day from waking up till going to sleep. A healthy routine includes showering, washing hands with soap, brushing teeth twice, drinking 6–8 glasses of water, eating, sleeping at least 8 hours and playing outside — some of these more than once a day.
Brush 2 times · water 6–8 glasses · sleep at least 8 hours
Rinse after eating; wash hands after toilet and outdoors
If a habit is hard, plan how to make it a habit

notes.h: Tracking My Habits — Health Table and 24-Hour Circle
items: Feelings like sleepy, hungry or tired are the body's way of telling us something is amiss. A weekly health table shows how our habits make us feel, and a 24-slice circle shows how we spend the 24 hours of a day.
Feelings are the body's messages
Health table = 7 days × habits + feeling
Circle = 24 slices = 24 hours
Wrong: If my hands look clean, they are clean. Right: Germs are too small to see — wash hands with soap even when they look clean (added)
Wrong: Only a toothbrush can clean teeth. Right: A datun twig also removes food stuck between teeth and even massages the gums
Wrong: Cleaners can only be bought from a shop. Right: We can make an eco-friendly cleaner at home from orange or lemon peels
Wrong: Breathing fast and sweating after running means I am ill. Right: It happens because exercise makes the heart work harder — it is good for the body
Wrong: A stranger who says 'your mother sent me' is safe to go with. Right: Say 'No, I don't know you' — go only with people you know or who know the family password
Wrong: Each habit is done only once a day. Right: Some are done more than once — brushing twice, rinsing after every meal, washing hands many times

sol_items: Write the activities you do every day from waking up to...: Shower, wash hands, brush teeth, drink 6 to 8 glasses of water, eat, play outside and sleep at least 8 hours.
Ask elders what they used to wash hair, body, clothes a...: Reetha, shikakai, datun (neem or babool twigs). Some can still be found.
Observe how animals and insects around you clean t: Cats lick their fur, birds preen feathers, monkeys pick through each others fur.
Identify the games shown (top, ludo, snakes and ladders...: Top and carrom: indoor or outdoor; ludo and snakes and ladders: indoor board games. Say which you have played.
Find the game names in the word search: Find them in the grid; name your favourites.
Which places are safe to play? Why or why not?: Safe: park and schoolground. Not safe: busy road, roof without railings, construction site, because we can get hurt.
imp_items: Why do monkeys pick through each others fur?
To keep their bodies free from insects
Name three habits that keep the body clean.
Brushing teeth, washing hands with soap, keeping nails trimmed
What is a datun?
A twig of neem, babool or karanj used to clean teeth
Why did Moyna prefer the babool twig?
Neem was too bitter; babool tasted better
How much home-cleaner do you mix in one bucket of water?
One cup
What do we need to make a home-cleaner from peels?
Orange or lemon peels and vinegar, kept in the sun for two weeks

subject: EVS
title: This World of Things
intro: In Class 3 EVS Chapter 10, This World of Things, the topics are: Things Are Made of Materials, where do materials come from?, transparent, translucent and opaque, how materials look, feel and sound, hard and rigid or soft and flexible, solid, liquid and gas, natural and artificial things. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Things Are Made of Materials
Every thing around us is made of some material — wood, metal, glass, plastic, cloth, clay or rubber
Where Do Materials Come From?
Materials come from nature: wood from trees, metals from ore dug from inside the Earth, glass mostly from sand; every material ...
Transparent, Translucent and Opaque
Some materials let us see through them clearly (transparent), some only partially (translucent), and some not at all (opaque)
How Materials Look, Feel and Sound
Materials also differ in how they feel (smooth or rough, cold to the touch), how they look (shiny or dull) and how they sound ...
Hard and Rigid or Soft and Flexible
Some materials are hard and rigid (wood), others soft and flexible (fabric)
Solid, Liquid and Gas
Things that keep their shape are solids; liquids like water flow and stay in a cup; gases like air flow and float in and out of a ...
Natural and Artificial Things
Things that exist in nature are natural — living (plants, animals) or not living (rocks, water, air)

items: Every thing around us is made of some material — wood, metal, glass, plastic, cloth, clay or rubber. One thing can be made of more than one material.
Things around us are made of materials.
Common materials: wood, metal, glass, plastic, cloth, clay, rubber.
We can group objects by the material they are made of.

Materials come from nature: wood from trees, metals from ore dug from inside the Earth, glass mostly from sand; every material can be traced back to something from nature (added). The materials people use also change over time.
Wood ← tree; metal ← ore from the Earth; glass ← mostly sand.
Every material can be traced back to nature (added).
Materials used for things change over time.
Some materials let us see through them clearly (transparent), some only partially (translucent), and some not at all (opaque).
Transparent — see clearly; translucent — see partially; opaque — cannot see.
Most glass is transparent; wood is opaque.
Never look at the sun.

notes.h: How Materials Look, Feel and Sound
items: Materials also differ in how they feel (smooth or rough, cold to the touch), how they look (shiny or dull) and how they sound when tapped — so we can recognise many materials even with our eyes closed.
Materials differ in feel, look and sound.
Metal is usually smooth, shiny, cold to touch and rings when tapped.
Use more than one sense to recognise a material.

notes.h: Hard and Rigid or Soft and Flexible
items: Some materials are hard and rigid (wood), others soft and flexible (fabric). This property decides which material suits which object.
Wood is hard and rigid; fabric is soft and flexible.
The property decides the use.
Odd pairs show why a material will not work.
Things that keep their shape are solids; liquids like water flow and stay in a cup; gases like air flow and float in and out of a cup.
Solid — keeps its shape.
Liquid — flows, stays in a cup.
Gas — flows, does not stay in a cup.
Things that exist in nature are natural — living (plants, animals) or not living (rocks, water, air). Things made by people are artificial.
Natural — not made by humans (living or not living).
Artificial — made by people.
Ask: who made the THING?
Wrong: A thing is made of only one material. Right: Many things use more than one material — a door is wood with metal hinges; a bulb is glass with a metal base
Wrong: Glass and metal are made in shops or factories from nothing. Right: Factories only change natural things: glass is made mostly from sand, metals are taken out of ore from the Earth
Wrong: Translucent means you cannot see anything through it. Right: Translucent lets you see partially — light or a blurred shape; opaque shows nothing
Wrong: Anything shiny must be metal. Right: Shiny paint can make wood or plastic shine too — check the sound and the cold feel as well
Wrong: A good material is good for everything. Right: Fabric is perfect for clothes but useless for a table — a material suits a job because of its properties
Wrong: Ice is a liquid because it is made of water. Right: Ice keeps its shape, so it is a solid

sol_items: Can you see through the window glass? Why?: Yes, because glass is transparent.
Which metals do you recognise around you?: Iron, copper, aluminium, steel, brass.
What are mats, bulbs and electric switches made of: Mats: cloth or plastic. Bulbs: glass and metal. Switches: plastic and metal.
Does your window have a glass pane? Can you see th: Yes. I can see the trees and the road outside.
Name one more transparent material: Clear plastic or water.
Find some translucent materials: Tracing paper, frosted glass, a paper lampshade.
imp_items: What is a material?
What a thing is made of, such as wood or metal
What is an alloy? Give one example.
A mixture of metals, such as steel or brass
Where do wood, metal and glass come from?
Wood from trees, metal from ore in the Earth, glass mostly from sand
What is ore?
Rock dug from the Earth from which metals are extracted
What does translucent mean? Give an example.
We see only partly through it, like tracing paper
How can you tell a metal spoon from a wooden one with eyes closed?
Metal feels cold and rings when tapped; wood feels warmer and gives a dull sound

subject: EVS
title: Making Things
intro: In Class 3 EVS Chapter 11, Making Things, the topics are: Clay — What Pots Are Made Of, how a potter makes a pot, patterns in nature and on pots, bricks — from mud to building, kinds of houses and what they are made of, safety first at work. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Clay — What Pots Are Made Of
Many things around us — pots, piggy banks, cups, bricks, statues — are made of clay
How a Potter Makes a Pot

notes.h: Clay — What Pots Are Made Of
items: Many things around us — pots, piggy banks, cups, bricks, statues — are made of clay. Clay is clean, wet, soft soil that can be shaped and keeps its shape when it dries.
Pots, gullak, kulhad, birdbath, bricks and many statues are made of clay.
Clay is made from wet soil cleaned with a sieve and soaked in water.
Wet clay can be shaped; dried clay keeps its shape.

notes.h: How a Potter Makes a Pot
items: A potter turns clay into a pot in 7 steps: (1) wet the clay, (2) pound it, (3) knead it like dough, (4) shape it on a spinning wheel, (5) dry it, (6) bake it in a very hot oven called a kiln, (7) decorate some pots with patterns.
Wet → pound → knead → shape on wheel → dry → bake in kiln → decorate.
The kiln is the potter’s very hot oven.
Baking makes the pot hard and ready for use.

notes.h: Patterns in Nature and on Pots
items: A pattern is a shape, line or colour that repeats. Patterns are everywhere in nature — leaves, spots, stripes — and artists who paint pots take their ideas from them.
A pattern repeats.
Patterns are seen on plants, animals and things.
Artists get ideas from nature to paint pots.
Bricks are made of mud like pots, but are shaped in moulds and then baked hard in a kiln. Laid one by one, with each brick resting on two below, they become strong walls and big buildings.
Bricks = mud + mould + kiln.
Bricks build houses, schools and hospitals.
Overlapping bricks make a sturdy wall.

notes.h: Kinds of Houses and What They Are Made Of
items: Not all houses are made of bricks. People build with what suits their weather and place — mud, grass and wood in warm areas, cloth for tents, wood for houseboats, cement and glass for tall buildings.
Different places → different houses.
Mud houses keep cool and use natural materials.
Houses can be made of bricks, mud, wood, cloth, cement, glass.

Builders follow safety rules: a helmet with a strap, a safety vest and sturdy footwear (and gloves, goggles and a mask) protect the body from falling things, accidents and dust. Homes and schools have safety rules too.
Helmet, vest, sturdy footwear — the book’s three.
Each item guards a part of the body.
Rules keep us safe at work, home and school.
Wrong: Any soil dug from the ground is ready to make pots. Right: Soil must be cleaned of pebbles, sand and leaves and soaked first; only then is it smooth clay
Wrong: A pot is ready as soon as it is shaped on the wheel. Right: It must first dry and then be baked in the kiln, or it stays soft and breaks
Wrong: Patterns are only drawings made by people. Right: Nature has patterns too — leopard spots, zebra stripes, leaves on a branch
Wrong: Bricks are cut out of stone. Right: Bricks are made of mud, shaped in a mould and baked hard
Wrong: All houses are made of bricks. Right: Houses are also made of mud, grass, wood, cloth, cement and glass
Wrong: The helmet strap is not needed. Right: Without the strap the helmet can fall off when you bend or something hits it

sol_items: Who has made them and how?: A potter, by shaping wet clay on a wheel, drying it and baking it in a kiln.
What are pots used for?: To store water, cook food and keep grains; also for plants.
What other things do potters make?: Cups, diyas, kulhads, piggy banks and toys.
Why is the pot baked in a kiln?: The great heat makes the clay hard and strong.
Make your own clay; make two things and dry them i: Clean the soil, soak it, knead it, shape two things and dry them.
Arrange the pot-making pictures in order: Wet clay, pound, knead, shape on wheel, dry, bake in kiln.
imp_items: Name three things made of clay.
Pot, gullak, kulhad
Why do we remove pebbles and leaves from the soil?
So the clay is smooth and can be shaped without cracks
What is a kiln?
The potter very hot oven
Why is the pot baked in a kiln?
The heat makes the clay hard and strong
What is a pattern?
Shapes, lines or colours that repeat
How do artists get ideas for their art?
From nature

items: Our own everyday activities — eating packed food, using things up, wearing out clothes — create a lot of waste. When it is not managed, it ends up in garbage piles near our homes and schools.
Everyday activities create waste.
Waste that is just thrown away piles up around us.
Managing waste is in our own hands — each one of us must learn it.
Waste left on roadsides and in open places harms animals, fills the air with harmful gases when plastic is burnt, and makes people ill through mosquitoes and germs in wastewater.
Plastic with food can kill animals.
Burning plastic gives harmful gases.
Wastewater puddles → mosquitoes → diseases; wastewater also carries germs.
Some places have cleaned up — so waste can be managed.

Reduce means making less waste in the first place — the first rule of managing waste. Buy only what we need, use it till it is no longer usable, carry cloth bags and avoid wrappers and plastic bottles.
Reduce is the FIRST rule.
The more we buy, the more waste.
Cloth bags, no wrappers, no plastic bottles.
Share old toys and books.
Reuse means using things again instead of throwing them away — the second thing people do to manage waste. Old clothes, paper, bottles, boxes and tyres can get a new job.
Reuse is the SECOND thing.
Old clothes → quilts, bags, give to the needy.
Paper → rough work, gift wrap, paper bag.
Steel or copper bottle, refilled.
Waste is separated into two dustbins: green for things that rot easily (they become compost for the soil) and blue for metal, glass, plastic and paper (they are recycled into new objects).
Green = rots easily → compost.
Blue = metal, glass, plastic, paper → recycling.
Recycling = new objects from thrown-away materials.
Wrap broken glass and needles.

Many villages and cities once had garbage everywhere, but their people changed them into some of the cleanest places in India — Silluk, a 'zero waste village' in Arunachal Pradesh, Chhota Narena, Indore and Mysuru.
Silluk = zero waste village (Arunachal Pradesh).
Chhota Narena = one of the first waste-free villages.
Indore and Mysuru = clean cities.
People changed their places by managing waste.
Each one of us can help keep our home, neighbourhood, school, city and country clean — with daily habits, cleaning tools and the National Cleanliness Day pledge: Want not, Waste not.
Each one of us can help.
National Cleanliness Day = 30 January.
Pledge: less waste, manage waste, dispose properly.
Want not, Waste not.
Wrong: Waste comes only from factories or from other people. Right: Our own everyday activities — eating, studying, shopping — create a lot of waste
Wrong: Burning plastic is a good way to get rid of it. Right: Burning plastic releases harmful gases into the air we breathe
Wrong: Buying many new things is fine if we put the old ones in the dustbin. Right: The more we buy, the more we throw away and the more waste is created
Wrong: Old things are useless; only new things are good. Right: Old sarees become quilts, old clothes become bags, newspaper becomes gift wrap and paper bags
Wrong: All waste can go into one dustbin. Right: Separate it: green-bin waste becomes compost, blue-bin waste goes for recycling
Wrong: Clean places were always clean. Right: They once had garbage littered all around; their people changed them

sol_items: What are the children and the teacher doing in the: They are cleaning the park.
Why are they cleaning the park?: To keep it clean and safe for everyone.
Have you thought how this waste is created?: By our everyday activities such as eating packed food and using things up.
Recall your daily activities: how do they create waste ...: Eating makes wrappers and peels; studying makes paper scraps. We throw them in a bin or on the road.
Draw a locality and circle garbage, wastewater or smoke...: Waste gets there when people throw it out. A clean place manages waste by sorting and collecting it.
How can you help in reducing waste?: Buy only what we need, use things fully and avoid wrappers.
imp_items: What is waste?
Things we throw away because we do not need them any more
Where does waste go when we just throw it away?
It ends up in garbage piles near our homes and schools
Why can a cow die near a garbage pile?
It may eat plastic mixed with food
How can wastewater on the road make people ill?
Mosquitoes increase and spread disease; the water also carries germs
Why is reduce the first rule?
Waste that is never made never has to be managed
Name two ways to reduce waste at school.
Carry a steel bottle and tiffin; avoid packed snacks
